Title: A TALL HAT WITH A SECRET
CustomInstruction: What does this invention do? Give it your best guess: accurate, absurd or brilliant.
AnswerDetails: Real answer: a "hat to prevent drowning": a top hat with a sealed, waterproof air space in the crown and a waterproof lining that pulls out by a cord into an air bag, patented by Samuel W. White, 1840 (US patent 1,826). A wearer who fell in the water pulled the cord to draw the lining out, held the neck of the bag and pulled the hat down under the water, where the trapped air kept him afloat. White was an Englishman, from Dorset, patenting his idea in the United States.
RealAnswer: A life-saving top hat: a waterproof air space in the crown, and a lining you pull out by a cord to make an air bag to hold onto

Title: A DOME FOR YOUR DOME

AnswerDetails: Real answer: a sunshade hat with a ribbed, umbrella-like canopy over a ventilated mesh crown, patented by Stephen B. Bartine, 1883 (US patent 276,753). RealAnswer: A ventilated sunshade hat: an umbrella-like ribbed canopy held above a mesh crown to keep the head cool

AnswerDetails: Real answer: a safety hood ("breathing device") whose long tube draws cleaner air from near the ground, patented by Garrett A. Morgan, 1914 (US patent 1,113,675). In 1916 Morgan wore his hood to help rescue workers trapped by gas in a tunnel under Lake Erie in Cleveland.
RealAnswer: A safety hood for breathing in smoke or fumes, its long tube drawing cleaner air from near the floor

AnswerDetails: Real answer: a cabinet bed, a roll-top desk that unfolds into a bed, patented by Sarah E. Goode, 1885 (US patent 322,177). RealAnswer: A desk that folds out into a full-size bed

Title: CONE, LEVER AND TONGS

AnswerDetails: Real answer: the ice-cream scoop ("ice-cream mold and disher"), patented by Alfred L. Cralle, 1897 (US patent 576,395). RealAnswer: The ice-cream scoop: squeeze the handle and a scraper frees a neat ball from the cone-shaped mould

Title: ROCK AND... WHAT?

AnswerDetails: Real answer: a combined rocking chair and fan, the rocking motion working a fan above the sitter, patented by C. Horst, 1847 (US patent 5,231). The arm curving over the chair carries a fan blade driven by the chair itself, so the harder you rock, the cooler you get.
RealAnswer: A rocking chair that works a fan over your head as you rock

Title: A CHAIR THAT WANTS ATTENTION
CustomInstruction: What does this invention do? Give it your best guess: accurate, absurd or brilliant.
AnswerDetails: Real answer: the "gong and signal chair for hotels": press a button and a gong sounds and a signal shows which seat wants service, patented by Miriam E. She proposed the chair for the House of Representatives, which later adopted a similar signal for calling its pages.
RealAnswer: A chair for hotels with a button that rings a gong and raises a signal, so a waiter knows which seat called

Title: THIS BOAT HAS A PLAN

AnswerDetails: Real answer: a device for "buoying vessels over shoals": inflatable chambers along the hull that lift a stranded boat, patented by Abraham Lincoln, 1849 (US patent 6,469). RealAnswer: Inflatable air chambers fitted to a boat's sides to lift it over sandbars in shallow rivers

Title: A POST WITH OPINIONS

AnswerDetails: Real answer: a traffic signal: a post at a crossroads with T-shaped arms showing STOP and GO, plus a position that halts traffic in every direction, patented by Garrett A. He sold the rights to General Electric.
RealAnswer: A traffic signal on a post, with arms that swing out to tell each direction of traffic to stop or go

Title: TWO BIKES ARE BETTER THAN ONE?

AnswerDetails: Real answer: a "double bicycle for looping the loop", built for a loop track with a gap in it, patented by Karl Lange, 1905 (US patent 790,063). RealAnswer: A trick bicycle with a second pair of wheels on top, for leaping the gap in a broken loop track upside down and riding out head-down

Title: WINTER, SOLVED?
CustomInstruction: What does this invention do? Give it your best guess: accurate, absurd or brilliant.
AnswerDetails: Real answer: the windscreen wiper ("window-cleaning device"), worked by a lever from inside the vehicle, patented by Mary Anderson, 1903 (US patent 743,801). RealAnswer: The windscreen wiper: a lever inside the vehicle swings a rubber blade across the glass

Title: SEE ANYTHING ODD?

AnswerDetails: Real answer: eye protectors for chickens, patented by Andrew Jackson Jr., 1903 (US patent 730,918). Two little lens frames, held on by a springy band over the head, shield the bird's eyes from flock-mates' pecks. Chicken spectacles really were sold to poultry keepers for decades.
RealAnswer: Spectacles for chickens, to protect their eyes from being pecked by other chickens

RealAnswer: A tiny timer camera strapped to a carrier pigeon's chest, taking aerial photos in flight

Title: HOLD STILL, BESSIE
CustomInstruction: What does this invention do? Give it your best guess: accurate, absurd or brilliant.
AnswerDetails: Real answer: a cow-tail holder, clamping the tail to the leg during milking, patented by James M. Worden, 1875 (US patent 159,490). Anyone who has milked by hand knows the problem: a cow's tail swatting flies tends to land on the milker. This strap and clamp kept it out of the way.
RealAnswer: A clamp that holds a cow's tail to her leg, so she cannot swish it in the milker's face

Title: A WHEEL FOR A WORKER

AnswerDetails: Real answer: a "dog-power", a tilted treadwheel a dog walks on to drive small machinery such as a butter churn, patented by David E. Pangburn, 1874 (US patent 154,075). RealAnswer: A dog-powered treadwheel: the dog walks on the tilted wheel and turns a shaft that can run small farm machines

Title: ROUND AND ROUND THE BOARD

RealAnswer: The Landlord's Game, the board game that became Monopoly

Title: THE MACHINE IN THE HALL
